sentences.text: The one she wanted was the face.
She had found it on the first night — third along the rafter, near the chimney breast — and she had gone back to it every night since, and every night the same thing happened.
She would look at it and think *oh, that's* — and then the name would not arrive.
It was a man.
Middle-aged, or getting there.
Dark hair going back at the front.
He was looking slightly to the left of whoever was dreaming him, and he was in the middle of saying something, and his eyebrows were up.
It was painted better than the others.
That was the strange part.
The kitchen and the boat and the green door were all painted the way a thing is painted from memory — the important bits sharp, everything else vague.

This one had a collar on his shirt with a button missing at the point, and a small scar through one eyebrow, and the sort of detail you only get when somebody has looked at a face for years and years and years.
She asked her uncle who it was.
He came up and looked at it for a while with his hands in his pockets and said he had no idea, and that he had been wondering about that one himself since about 2003.
She did the sensible thing, which took her three weeks.
She drew it — badly, then less badly, then on the fourth attempt well enough to be recognisable — and she carried the drawing round the town in her coat pocket and showed it to people.
The woman at the bakery said no.
The man at the bicycle shop said no, and then held the drawing at arm's length and said no again, more slowly.
The librarian said he looked like somebody's brother, which was not useful.
Father Costa said he looked like everybody's brother, which was less useful still.
A man at the bus stop said it was a very good drawing, which she appreciated but could not do anything with.
At the end of three weeks she had shown it to thirty-one people and none of them knew him.
She sat on the wall outside the chemist with the drawing on her knee and worked it out, and she did not enjoy working it out.
There were only two ways it went.
Either the person who had dropped that dream had moved away — in which case the moth would sit on that rafter until the house fell down.

Or the person who had dropped it was dead, and the dream had come loose the way the last of anything comes loose, and it had come up the hill and in under the slates and folded itself against a beam, and there was nobody left in the world who could be given it.
She went home and up the ladder and sat on the edge of the hatch for a long time.
Her uncle came up eventually with the tea.
He did not ask how it had gone; he had clearly worked out how it had gone from the fact that she was sitting in the dark.
"There are about four hundred like that," he said.
"That I know of.
Ones nobody claims.
They don't go anywhere.

They don't die, as far as I can tell — I've got one up there with a horse and cart on it and there hasn't been a cart on this hill since before the war." "So what are they for?" "They're not *for* anything," he said.
"That's the bit that took me longest.
I spent about fifteen years trying to make this place useful and I got nowhere, because I was asking the wrong question." He nodded up at the rafters.
"It's not a lost property office.
Nobody's coming to the desk.
It's just where they end up." Ines looked at the man with his eyebrows up, in the middle of saying something, to somebody who had loved him enough to keep the missing button.
"That's sad," she said.
"It is," her uncle agreed.
"But look at the state of him.
Somebody was extremely fond of that man.
That's still true.
It's true right now, on that rafter, whether or not anybody comes for it." He drank his tea.
"There are worse things to have a house full of."
